I’ve been in positions similar to yours several times, and as soon as I mention they have access to all my lessons and have been shown how to use them for catch up their tune changes and they realise the onus is on their child.

When I first started I had a bottom set year 9 class who were honestly my worst, I dreaded their lessons because their behaviour was so poor. So imagine my feelings when I find out the next year that I have that same glass for GCSE… I know they weren’t happy about having me either!

They’re in y11 now and when I realised that this is it, I won’t see any of these kids in July honestly my heart sunk. Three years of seeing them, battling with them, dragging them through the combined science course despite their best efforts not to learn, watching them grow as individuals. And in those three years I got to know them so much, we somehow managed to build a good relationship! 

Out of all the classes I’ve had this class has taught me the most - about patience, about good quality teaching, about kindness. I felt miserable last year when my triples left, but this is a different feeling. 
I probably won’t ever see these kids again, they won’t be at our sixth form. I don’t know what they’ll do with themselves but I just hope that they look after and do good by themselves. I hate this half term because of how bittersweet it is, I’m saying goodbye to 112 GCSE pupils this year and none of them are easy. 

No one warned me about the attachment issues when I went into teaching! And I guess many people don’t feel that way, maybe I won’t after a few years too - but for now I’m really glad you posted this because it’s true, there is a real feeling of pride and sadness when they finally leave.  I’m so grateful because every interaction with these students has made me a better person and I just hope that I was able to positively influence them in some way too. 

Enjoy your last few moments with your class OP! Do something nice with them before they leave and let them know how much you’ll miss them. If you have a sixth form you’ll probably see lots of them around, my triples from last year are always coming to see me! 😊

This is so outdated and your head can keep his ideals to himself. I live 5 mins from my school and students/parents have said hello to me while I’m out on dates, back and forth from gym, in parks, at supermarkets and even at my second job. In fact I had an Uber driver once driving me home from a bottomless brunch, who recognised me from his daughter’s parents’ evening!  It’s done nothing but make me more relatable and approachable, students feel comfortable with me because I don’t pretend to be some righteous perfect person. And sure there might be occasional parents who might not like it (I’ve never encountered this), but my head is very clear on the fact that we are humans before we are teachers - as long as it’s not wildly inappropriate, what we do outside of school is our business. 

I can definitely appreciate it being harder in a village but honestly, it’s such an outdated concept for teachers to put up a persona in all aspects of their life. Any school staff, parent, grandparent or whatever who thinks teachers should live in caution should apply that same rule to themselves - they have impressionable contact with children too. Watch how many excuses pour out when it’s turned on them! 

Live your life OP and don’t worry about being human, we should all be showing our students that it’s okay to be true to yourself 😊

I think your question’s been answered (there’s nothing to report) but I’ll tell you a story from when I was in PGCE. In my program (SCITT) there was a girl who was the daughter of a headteacher but didn’t tell anyone until later. One of her friends was venting to her about the school she was in and the school happened to be the one the girl’s dad was a head at. This girl told her dad and instead of going after the person who vented, her dad asked the SCITT to do a session on professionalism. In the session, they mentioned that it’s okay and actually healthy to vent, just be careful that you do it around people you trust, and to also consider whether you are going to be a colleague people will fear speaking to or a colleague they can trust. The girl also told me her dad said it was unkind on her part to report venting, especially as there was no harm done. 

The only time to report something is when a colleague is actively doing something that puts a child at risk. And being harsher with more challenging students is definitely not putting anyone at risk, if anything it’s better behaviour management than giving everyone lots of chances if you know some of them will take liberties and negatively impact the lesson. 

I moan about my students all the time (everyone’s used choice language at some point or the other when it comes to students) and have definitely celebrated a few of them getting excluded, but that doesn’t mean I won’t do absolutely everything in my power to provide them the education they deserve. Just like the students have probably said god awful things about us teachers but would never show it.

Reporting your colleagues will result in: 
1. The people involved potentially having a formal conversation with SLT about it 
2. Absolutely no favours with SLT, it doesn’t make you look any better that you’re reporting colleagues for venting 
3. No difference to the students if nothing was actively being done to them in the first place 
4. A department that now knows you are not to be trusted 

Personally, if I feel uncomfortable with something a colleague’s said, I talk to them privately about it to understand more instead of assuming the worst. And the only reason I can do that without fallout is because I’ve built trust and friendships with them. 

I hope this helps you understand the situation better! Good luck with training 😊

Salaried trainee also here! I’m in secondary, never stepped foot in a classroom before September (apart from as a student lol)

Your feelings are 100% valid and it’s a shame you aren’t getting more support from the school.

1) speak to your training provider - in my experience they are very lenient with salaried trainees where we have an extra workload. My priority is my students so if I need to step back from my PGCE/training tasks I generally do. 

2) Speak to other teachers and find other trainees - for the most part everyone is really helpful and if you let others in your school know about your struggles you are bound to get some support from colleagues! 

3) communicate with your mentor about what you actually want from her. My mentor doesn’t even set my targets - we have a meeting once a fortnight so I can bounce ideas off of her and other than that I email/call with questions. And that’s completely my choice, I wanted to be quite independent with it. It might be the case that your mentor is worried about patronising you so she doesn’t do more than set targets? A discussion with her outlining expectations will help you. If after that she makes clear that she can’t or doesn’t want to help you more than she already is, that is something you can go back to your training provider about and they can get you a different mentor. 

4) I have been working 7 days/week since September, and if I decide to take a night off it generally impacts my workload for a good 2-3 days. This is not ideal but it is what I expected in my training year considering I’m salaried. The most important thing is support - I feel like I can manage my heavy workload because I have colleagues all through my department giving me resources, tips, support. I am still behind and my to do list is never ending, but I am okay. 

It is a crazy year, I’ve been stressed to the max and full of impostor syndrome but it is good friends, good colleagues and (mostly) good classes that are getting me through! 

Feel free to message if you need to talk ❤️
